summary: This lecture is the second part of the Isra' wal-Mi'raj, focused on what the Prophet ﷺ saw, heard and smelled on the journey. The ustaz recaps the stops and the prophets in the seven heavens, then reads Prophet Ibrahim's message that the ummah should plant more of Paradise through dhikr. He then explains authentic or hasan hadiths about the punishment of major sins: those who consume riba, those who leave the lawful for the unlawful, preachers who do not practise what they preach, backbiters and those who violate others' honour, those who consume orphans' wealth, and the choice of milk over wine. He also mentions Bilal RA whose footsteps were heard in Paradise and the story of Pharaoh's daughter's hairdresser who stood firm on the word of tawhid. The ustaz closes with the Prophet's ﷺ parable of a man holding moths back from jumping into a fire, and stresses that da'wah must be driven by love, not hatred.
keyPoints: The Prophet ﷺ did not merely witness punishment on the Isra' and Mi'raj, but returned with deeper compassion for people.
Prophet Ibrahim AS's message: plant more in Paradise through tasbih, tahmid, tahlil and takbir.
Every strict prohibition in the Shari'ah has social consequences, and the Prophet ﷺ saw the recompense for riba, zina, gossip, religious hypocrisy and consuming an orphan's wealth.
Whoever calls to good must keep integrity and not forget himself.
Bilal RA was raised for his steady wudu and prayer despite being a slave looked down upon.
Da'wah is driven by love for people and hatred of sin, not hatred of individuals.

chapters.title: Opening and dua for protection of blessings
chapters.summary: The ustaz begins with the Prophet's dua that blessings not be removed and that we not be struck by Allah's wrath suddenly.

chapters.title: Recap of part one and outline of the episode

chapters.title: The prophets in the seven heavens and Prophet Ibrahim's message
chapters.summary: Meeting the prophets strengthened the Prophet's resolve, and Prophet Ibrahim AS urged the ummah to plant Paradise through dhikr.

chapters.title: Understood only with the eyes of faith
chapters.summary: This event cannot be analysed scientifically, and the ustaz chooses only sahih, hasan or mildly weak hadiths.

chapters.title: The punishment of those who consume riba

chapters.title: Riba in the Qur'an and the Prophet's curse
chapters.summary: The gradual prohibition of riba, the threat of war from Allah and His Messenger, and the curse on all who are involved.

chapters.title: The social effects of riba and debt
chapters.summary: The ustaz describes how riba-based debt traps lives, makes marriage harder and burdens families.

chapters.title: Leaving the lawful for the unlawful
chapters.summary: The Prophet saw a people choosing rotten meat over good meat, like those who leave their lawful spouse for zina.

chapters.title: The branches of zina and their social effects
chapters.summary: The hadith on zina of the eye, ear, hand, foot and heart, and the danger of normalising a culture of sin.

chapters.title: Preachers who do not practise
chapters.summary: The Prophet saw a people whose lips were cut with fiery scissors, preachers who enjoin good but forget themselves.

chapters.title: The first three dragged into the Fire
chapters.summary: The Qur'an teacher, the philanthropist and the fighter who acted to be praised by people.

chapters.title: Backbiting and violating honour
chapters.summary: The people with copper nails clawing their own faces and chests are backbiters, with a warning to the media and cyber bullying.

chapters.title: An orphan's wealth and wine
chapters.summary: Those who consume an orphan's wealth swallow fire, and the Prophet chose milk over wine, which covers the mind.

chapters.title: Bilal ibn Rabah and his footsteps in Paradise
chapters.summary: Bilal RA kept his wudu and prayed whenever he made it, so the Prophet heard his footsteps in Paradise.

chapters.title: The hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter
chapters.summary: The fragrance the Prophet smelled was the story of a hairdresser and her children who held to La ilaha illallah until burned.

chapters.title: The parable of the moths and da'wah with love
chapters.summary: The Prophet is like a man holding moths back from the fire, and da'wah must be driven by love.

dalil.context: The dua the Prophet taught when we enjoy blessings and fear losing them.
dalil.translation: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the loss of Your blessing, the change of Your well-being, the sudden coming of Your wrath, and all Your displeasure.

dalil.context: A hadith graded sahih, and some scholars rate it hasan.
dalil.translation: Ibrahim said: O Muhammad, convey my greetings to your ummah and tell them Paradise is fertile in soil, sweet in water, wide and empty, and its seeds are Subhanallah, Alhamdulillah, La ilaha illallah and Allahu akbar.

dalil.context: The ustaz notes Prophet Ibrahim did not advise on worldly matters, only investment in Paradise.
dalil.translation: Ibrahim said: tell your ummah to increase the seeds of Paradise, namely the words of dhikr.

dalil.context: The ustaz says scholars of hadith grade this hasan.
dalil.translation: On the night I was taken on the Isra' I passed a people whose bellies were like houses, with snakes visible inside. Jibril said: they are the consumers of riba.

dalil.context: Allah commands the believers to fear Him and give up what remains of riba. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: You who believe, beware of God: give up any outstanding dues from usury, if you are true believers.

dalil.context: If they do not give up riba, Allah and His Messenger will war against them. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: If you do not, then be warned of war from God and His Messenger. You shall have your capital if you repent, and without suffering loss or causing others to suffer loss.

dalil.context: This hadith covers the many roles involved in riba.
dalil.translation: The Messenger of Allah cursed the consumer of riba, the one who feeds it, its writer and its two witnesses, and said they are alike.

dalil.context: The ustaz cites another hadith on the punishment of riba.
dalil.translation: The Prophet dreamed of a man swimming in a river of blood, and each time he reached the bank a stone was thrown into his mouth and he sank again, and he said this was the consumer of riba.

dalil.context: The ustaz reads rotten meat as unlawful relations and good meat as lawful marriage.
dalil.translation: I passed a people before whom lay fat good meat and rotten foul meat, yet they chose to eat the rotten. Jibril said: they leave what is lawful of women and go to what is unlawful.

dalil.context: The prohibition on approaching zina, for it is an indecency and an evil way. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: And do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage, and an evil path.

dalil.context: The ustaz links this to the danger of normalising looks, songs and jokes with sexual content.
dalil.translation: Allah has decreed for the son of Adam his share of zina which he will surely meet: the eye's zina is the look, the tongue's is speech, the hand's is touch, the foot's is walking, the heart wishes and hopes, and the private part confirms or denies it.

dalil.context: The ustaz says this hadith is sahih, and some scholars rate it hasan.
dalil.translation: I passed a people whose lips were cut with fiery scissors. Jibril said: they are the preachers and khatibs of your ummah who enjoin people to good but forget themselves, though they recite the Book. Do they not use reason?

dalil.context: Allah rebukes those who enjoin people to good but forget themselves though they recite the Book.
dalil.translation: How can you tell people to do what is right and forget to do it yourselves, even though you recite the Scripture? Have you no sense?

dalil.context: The ustaz warns especially those who hold the microphone in an age of pretence.
dalil.translation: The Qur'an teacher, the one who spent in charity and the one who died fighting each claim a good intention, but Allah says they lie, they acted to be called a scholar, generous or brave, and they are dragged on their faces into the Fire.

dalil.context: Linked to the prohibition of backbiting in Surah al-Hujurat.
dalil.translation: I passed a people with copper nails, clawing their own faces and chests. Jibril said: they are those who eat people's flesh and violate their honour.

dalil.context: The prohibition of backbiting with the image of eating the flesh of a dead brother. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Believers, avoid making too many assumptions- some assumptions are sinful- and do not spy on one another or speak ill of people behind their backs: would any of you like to eat the flesh of your dead brother? No, you would hate it. So be mindful of God: God is ever relenting, most merciful.

dalil.context: The threat of punishment in this world and the next for those who spread indecency among the believers. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: A painful punishment waits in this world and the next for those who like indecency to spread among the believers: God knows and you do not.

dalil.context: Those who consume an orphan's wealth unjustly only swallow fire into their bellies. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are actually swallowing fire into their own bellies: they will burn in the blazing Flame.

dalil.context: The ustaz says both narrations are sahih, and wine is called the mother of evils because it covers the mind.
dalil.translation: On the night of the Isra' two vessels were brought to me, one of wine and one of milk. I took the milk, and it was said: you have chosen the fitrah, had you taken wine your ummah would have gone astray.

dalil.context: A slight difference in the items offered between the two narrations.
dalil.translation: A vessel of milk, honey and wine was brought to the Prophet. He took the milk and drank it, and Jibril said: you have chosen the fitrah.

dalil.context: Bilal was a dark-skinned slave looked down upon, and the Prophet's muezzin.
dalil.translation: The Prophet heard Bilal's footsteps in Paradise and asked what deed he hoped for most. Bilal replied that he never made wudu by day or night without praying with it as much as Allah willed.

dalil.context: She said Bismillah when her comb fell, was threatened, and was burned with her children for refusing to abandon tawhid.
dalil.translation: On the night of the Isra' I smelled a very fragrant scent. Jibril said: this is the scent of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter and her children.

dalil.context: The ustaz says this hadith is strong and depicts the Prophet's love for his ummah.
dalil.translation: My likeness and the people's is like a man who kindled a fire, and when it lit up around him moths and insects flew into it. I hold you back from the fire, but you overpower me and plunge into it.

dalil.context: Allah rebukes those who say what they do not do. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: You who believe, why do you say things and then do not do them?

dalil.context: It is greatly hateful to Allah to say what you do not do. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: It is most hateful to God that you say things and then do not do them;

Source of the hadiths on the man in the river of blood, the zina of the son of Adam, milk and wine, Bilal and the parable of the moths.
Source of the hadiths on rotten meat, preachers with cut lips, Pharaoh's daughter's hairdresser and Ibrahim's message.
One of the sources of the hadith of riba consumers whose bellies are full of snakes.
A dull finance book because there are no shortcuts; it teaches restraint and not spending beyond one's means.
A book by a Christian woman who works with rape survivors and studies how the normalisation of zina came about.
A compilation of major sins with their evidences.
A collection of hadiths on character, backbiting, intention and deeds.

people.context: Welcomed the Prophet in the seventh heaven and sent greetings and the message to plant Paradise with dhikr.
Narrator of the hadith of riba consumers with bellies full of snakes.
Acts like a guide who answers the Prophet's questions about each person and thing he saw.

people.role: People who did not drink wine or worship idols
people.context: Among those like the Prophet before revelation in avoiding the harmful habits of their society.
Author of The Simple Path to Wealth.
Graded the hadith of good and rotten meat as hasan.
A Christian woman who helps rape survivors and wrote The Case Against the Sexual Revolution.
Exposed a priest who stole public donations and was threatened with death, then proven right.
Quoted as saying that one who seeks filth will find filth, because it reflects what is in the heart.

people.role: Muezzin of the Prophet and Companion
people.context: A dark-skinned slave looked down upon, whose footsteps the Prophet heard in Paradise for keeping his wudu and prayer.
Her name is unknown. Burned with her children for not abandoning tawhid, and the Prophet smelled her fragrance.
Punished the hairdresser and her children in secret, and the ustaz says dictators live hiding their fear.

lessons.title: Seek protection from the loss of blessings
lessons.body: When enjoying provision we recall it is from Allah and pray that it is not removed or punished suddenly.

lessons.title: This event is understood by faith, not scientific technique
lessons.body: The Isra' and Mi'raj touches matters of faith, so it cannot be fully explained through a scientific lens.

lessons.title: Every strict prohibition has social effects
lessons.body: When Allah prohibits something strongly, it carries great social consequences.

lessons.title: Social change must be gradual
lessons.body: Deeply rooted practices like riba are corrected in stages, not drastically.

lessons.title: Avoid every role in riba
lessons.body: Writers, witnesses, guarantors and all involved share the sin, so do not work in or take part in any part of it.

lessons.title: Do not make marriage hard with unnecessary spending
lessons.body: Expensive weddings burden couples with years of debt, so make it easy.

lessons.title: Stay away from zina and its doors
lessons.body: Do not approach zina, including looks, hearing, speech and the heart, and block habits that normalise it.

lessons.title: Religious figures must have integrity
lessons.body: The Prophet trained the Companions to be scholars who are the same in front of and behind people.

lessons.title: Purify intention and avoid pretence
lessons.body: Knowledge, charity and fighting are worth nothing if done to be called a scholar, generous or brave.

lessons.title: Guard your tongue and others' honour
lessons.body: Gossip, exposing flaws and spreading accusations violate honour, and work that depends on them should be left.

lessons.title: Protect an orphan's wealth
lessons.body: Orphans are the weakest and easily exploited, so beware their wealth and collections made in their name.

lessons.title: Wine covers the mind and removes shame
lessons.body: Khamr means covering, because it covers the mind until shame is lost and brings social harm.

lessons.title: Small steady deeds raise one's rank
lessons.body: Bilal kept his wudu and prayed whenever he made it, and Allah raised him though he was looked down on.

lessons.title: Da'wah is driven by love, not hate
lessons.body: We hate the sin but are not taught to hate the person, like the Prophet who held people back from the fire with compassion.

lessons.title: Help others while improving yourself
lessons.body: We do not wait to be perfect, but keep integrity while helping others out of traps.

glossary.meaning: A very weak hadith, which the ustaz does not include in this lecture.
A guide who leads pilgrims in tawaf, used here to describe Jibril's role.
An unlawful increase in a loan or exchange, whose consumer is threatened with punishment and curse.
Praying that someone be kept from Allah's mercy, a very high level of anger.
Sexual relations outside lawful marriage, which the Qur'an forbids even approaching.
One who delivers a religious sermon or talk.
Wine, from the sense of covering, because it covers the mind.
